extracted.intended_audience: general readers of humorous essays; writers interested in fiction and comic writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles relevant to producing short humorous literary essays and light fiction (characterization, economy of description, scene-contrast, comic anthropomorphism and timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe characters vaguely to allow reader projection
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is not policy to bind oneself too closely to detail. A wise friend of mine, who knows his business, describes his hero invariably in the vaguest terms.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let readers fill in specifics themselves so each reader can picture the hero as their own ideal; avoid exhaustive physical detail (height, exact shade of hair, etc.) that pins down the reader’s imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the protagonist agreeable ('Make the fellow nice')
rubrics_metrics.description: “Make the fellow nice,” is his advice. “Let every woman reader picture him to herself as her particular man. Then everything he says and does becomes of importance to her. She is careful not to miss a word.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a generally likeable or appealing central figure so readers emotionally invest and pay attention to his words and actions rather than rejecting him on a petty detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct heroines as composites ('a bit of every girl in her')
rubrics_metrics.description: “For the same reason he sees to it that his heroine has a bit of every girl in her.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build female characters by combining familiar, widely-recognized traits rather than hyper-specific types so they feel broadly recognizable and relatable to many readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use economy of description — ‘dashing off in a few bold strokes’
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nowadays we content ourselves—and our readers also, I am inclined to think—with dashing her off in a few bold strokes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor evocative, concise imagery and suggestion over long, minute description; a few strong details can produce a vivid impression without bogging the narrative down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid needless padding — ensure scenes advance the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The author complains that long serial chapters are often boiled down by sub-editors: “a week’s unnecessary work on the part of the author boiled down to its essentials.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that chapters or scenes that merely repeat stock material or fill space can be perceived as unnecessary; aim for each installment or episode to contribute plot, character, or humor rather than idle repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t rely solely on stock 'smart talk' and repeated clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece lampoons predictable dialogue and types: “Much smart talk is indulged in.” and notes recurring conventional figures (the Duchess, the proverb-obsessed young lady, the disgraceful old Peer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stock witty exchanges and recurring stock characters can feel stale; refresh familiar comic types with specific twists or sharper originality to keep them amusing rather than tired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visual and social contrast for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: On the tennis ground: “It was an odd contrast; the two worlds divided by that wire fencing—so slight, almost invisible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place contrasting elements (social classes, settings, costumes, activities) side-by-side to create a striking picture that yields gentle irony or visual comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ anthropomorphism and miniature vignettes for humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator gives long comic scenes of swallows and sparrows speaking and behaving like people (stealing nests, arguing, choosing ‘colour schemes’): e.g., Mrs. Sparrow’s ‘apple-blossom pink and Reckitt’s blue’ interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant animals human motives, dialogue, and petty domestic concerns to craft charming, small-scale comic episodes that reflect human foibles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stretch or delay action for comic timing and emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated by the tennis player who lofts the ball sky-high and the waiting opponent: the ball ‘went a hundred feet... Newcomers would chatter... He would wave them aside... When it was at the proper height he would hit it back,’ producing prolonged, absurd situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use patient buildup, intentional delay, and prolonged small embarrassments to create comic tension and payoff; allowing a moment to linger can make the eventual joke or reversal funnier.
